summary: Chapter 90 has 15 verses in the Charles text. The chapter moves from And I saw till that in this manner thirty-five shepherds undertook the pasturing (of the sheep), and they severally comp to And I saw till the Lord of the sheep came unto them in wrath, and all who saw Him fled, and they all fell †into His shad, carrying forward the Parables' courtroom or the Luminaries' inventory and entrusting its secrets to Enoch for preservation.
whyItMatters: It advances Enoch's apocalyptic claim that judgment and cosmic order are entrusted together to the righteous for preservation.

context.author: Pseudonymously attributed to Enoch; modern scholarship sees distinct booklets composed in Aramaic and later rendered through Greek into Ge'ez
context.audience: Jewish readers under Hellenistic pressure and later the Ethiopian Orthodox Church that preserves the complete Ge'ez book
context.date: Booklets from the third century BC to the first century AD; the Ge'ez collection preserved from late antiquity and copied from the fifteenth century onward
context.setting: From Mount Hermon and the wilderness to the heavenly throne room and the chambers of the luminaries, narrated as Enoch's tours and dreams
context.literaryForm: Parable or apocalyptic courtroom vision (55–71) and, in chapter 72, calendrical inventory — revelation by tour, measure, and recited book

keyVerses.text: And I saw till that in this manner thirty-five shepherds undertook the pasturing (of the sheep), and they severally completed their periods as did the first; and others received them into their hands, to pasture them for their period, each shepherd in his own period.
keyVerses.why: This opening verse establishes the chapter's setting — time, place, or speaker — and without it the elaborate visions lack their narrative foothold.

keyVerses.text: And I saw in the vision how the ravens flew upon those lambs and took one of those lambs, and dashed the sheep in pieces and devoured them.
keyVerses.why: The middle of the chapter typically pronounces the verdict or the inventory's central law, distilling the theological or calendrical claim the other verses support.

keyVerses.text: And I saw till the Lord of the sheep came unto them in wrath, and all who saw Him fled, and they all fell †into His shadow† from before His face. || 17. And I saw that man, who wrote the book according to the command of the Lord, till he opened that book concerning the destruction which those twelve last shepherds had wrought, and showed that they had destroyed much more than their predecessors, before the Lord of the sheep. 18. And I saw till the Lord of the sheep came unto them and took in His hand the staff of His wrath, and smote the earth, and the earth clave asunder, and all the beasts and all the birds of the heaven fell from among those sheep, and were swallowed up in the earth and it covered them. |} 20. And I saw till a throne was erected in the pleasant land, and the Lord of the sheep sat Himself thereon, and the other took the sealed books and opened those books before the Lord of the sheep. 21. And the Lord called those men the seven first white ones, and commanded that they should bring before Him, beginning with the first star which led the way, all the stars whose privy members were like those of horses, and they brought them all before Him. 22. And He said to that man who wrote before Him, being one of those seven white ones, and said unto him: ‘Take those seventy shepherds to whom I delivered the sheep, and who taking them on their own authority slew more than I commanded them.’ 23. And behold they were all bound, I saw, and they all stood before Him. 24. And the judgement was held first over the stars, and they were judged and found guilty, and went to the place of condemnation, and they were cast into an abyss, full of fire and flaming, and full of pillars of fire. 25. And those seventy shepherds were judged and found guilty, and they were cast into that fiery abyss. 26. And I saw at that time how a like abyss was opened in the midst of the earth, full of fire, and they brought those blinded sheep, and they were all judged and found guilty and cast into this fiery abyss, and they burned; now this abyss was to the right of that house. 27. And I saw those sheep burning †and their bones burning†. 28. And I stood up to see till they folded up that old house; and carried off all the pillars, and all the beams and ornaments of the house were at the same time folded up with it, and they carried it off and laid it in a place in the south of the land. 29. And I saw till the Lord of the sheep brought a new house greater and loftier than that first, and set it up in the place of the first which had been folded up: all its pillars were new, and its ornaments were new and larger than those of the first, the old one which He had taken away, and all the sheep were within it. 30. And I saw all the sheep which had been left, and all the beasts on the earth, and all the birds of the heaven, falling down and doing homage to those sheep and making petition to and obeying them in every thing. 31. And thereafter those three who were clothed in white and had seized me by my hand [who had taken me up before], and the hand of that ram also seizing hold of me, they took me up and set me down in the midst of those sheep †before the judgement took place†. 32. And those sheep were all white, and their wool was abundant and clean. 33. And all that had been destroyed and dispersed, and all the beasts of the field, and all the birds of the heaven, assembled in that house, and the Lord of the sheep rejoiced with great joy because they were all good and had returned to His house. 34. And I saw till they laid down that sword, which had been given to the sheep, and they brought it back into the house, and it was sealed before the presence of the Lord, and all the sheep were invited into that house, but it held them not. 35. And the eyes of them all were opened, and they saw the good, and there was not one among them that did not see. 36. And I saw that that house was large and broad and very full. 37. And I saw that a white bull was born, with large horns, and all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the air feared him and made petition to him all the time. 38. And I saw till all their generations were transformed, and they all became white bulls; and the first among them became a lamb, and that lamb became a great animal and had great black horns on its head; and the Lord of the sheep rejoiced over it and over all the oxen. 39. And I slept in their midst: and I awoke and saw everything. 40. This is the vision which I saw while I slept, and I awoke and blessed the Lord of righteousness and gave Him glory. 41. Then I wept with a great weeping and my tears stayed not till I could no longer endure it: when I saw, they flowed on account of what I had seen; for everything shall come and be fulfilled, and all the deeds of men in their order were shown to me. 42. On that night I remembered the first dream, and because of it I wept and was troubled—because I had seen that vision.
keyVerses.why: The closing verse signals the author's purpose — exhortation, commission, or doxology — and shows how the revelation is meant to be kept and transmitted.

questions.question: What is actually happening in 1 Enoch 90, and who is speaking or being shown something?
questions.answer: In this chapter the seer Enoch is shown a further stage of the visions that began in chapter 37. The voice or angelic guide presents a specific judgment or heavenly order, and Enoch records what is said and seen so it can be transmitted. The chapter's 15 verses move from announcement to its content and then to its effect on those who hear it.

questions.question: What key title or image appears here — for example Head of Days, Lord of Spirits, or Son of Man / Elect One — and how does Charles render it?
questions.answer: Charles keeps the book's distinctive titles — Head of Days for the enthroned Ancient One and Elect One or Son of Man for the heavenly assessor — with initial capitals so the repetition is visible. In this chapter the title signals which courtroom participant is speaking or being enthroned, not merely a poetic flourish, and the briefing explains that the three names for the assessor describe one office.

questions.question: Why does the chapter link the fate of 'kings and the mighty' to a throne or judgment?
questions.answer: Parables chapters repeatedly stage a reversal: those who felt secure on earth — kings, the exalted, those who dwell on the earth — are summoned before the Head of Days and the Elect One. The judgment is not a private opinion but a courtroom scene with a throne, and the verdict exposes that earthly power does not survive the heavenly audit.

questions.question: How does this chapter compare to Daniel 7 or Genesis 6, which share throne and Watcher material?
questions.answer: Daniel 7 supplies the throne and Ancient of Days / son-of-man background that the Parables reuses with its Head of Days and Son of Man, while Genesis 6:1-4 supplies the sons-of-God entry point that the Watcher story expands. This chapter should be read alongside those passages as reuse, not proof — a cross-reference is a route for comparison, not evidence that two texts mean the same thing.

questions.question: What does the chapter expect from its readers — warning, comfort, or instruction about time?
questions.answer: Like other Enoch booklets, the chapter ends not with curiosity alone but with a stance for the righteous: trust that the judgment is certain, refrain from the Watchers' transgression, and keep the revealed instruction. Even calendrical or astronomical details aim at practice — counting days faithfully and preserving the book for children — rather than speculation.

questions.question: A hard verse: does this chapter teach that God 'repented' or that angels literally hold scourges and chains?
questions.answer: In 55:1 the Head of Days 'repented' translates a Semitic idiom for a decisive turn, not that God learns something new, and in chapters like 56 the angels of punishment with scourges and chains are courtroom imagery for assured execution of sentence. Readers differ on how literally to picture such agents, but the text's point is certainty of judgment, not a material description of heavenly ironwork.

questions.question: Where does the Charles English show its editorial marks — ⌈⌉ or [ ] — and why are they kept?
questions.answer: Charles uses ⌈⌉ for conjectured readings and [ ] for words he supplies to make sense of the Ge'ez, and the hosted text preserves them verbatim. They signal where the Ge'ez–Greek chain is thin, inviting caution rather than filling the gap with a confident paraphrase. The book briefing's textual history explains that no complete Hebrew original survives.

questions.question: How does this small unit connect to the larger anthology — Watchers, Parables, Luminaries, Dream Visions, or Epistle?
questions.answer: Chapters 55-71 sit at the seam where the second Parable closes and the Parables as a whole approach Enoch's elevation, while chapter 72 opens the entirely different Luminaries inventory. This chapter therefore participates in the anthology's cumulative claim: judgment in heaven and order in the heavens belong to one moral world, and both are entrusted to Enoch to write down.
